# Mode System Prompts Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

The system prompt each mode sends, which tells the harness what kind of work a prompt is, and which each project can make its own.

### Shape

#### Description

What a prompt tells the harness besides itself comes in two parts. The system template is the conversation's system prompt: the same for every prompt of a conversation, whatever its mode, so the harness's prompt cache holds when the mode changes. Each lane's tasks, and the questions, carry on a conversation of their own, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says, and each fills the system template in for what its runs can see, so it stays the same within each. Each of the [PromptModesScope](../modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope) but Freeform has instructions of its own, which change from one prompt to the next, and so go in the prompt's own message, in a block marked <task-instructions> at its head. A prompt's hidden anchor has a systemPrompt property, alongside its userPrompt, holding its mode's instructions.

#### Templates

The system template, each mode's instructions, and the injected prompts are Piton prose, like the prompt they are sent with, so they can reference the spec, with these placeholders, each written after a dollar sign and inside braces like a Piton interpolation:

- CODE_LOCATION and SPEC_LOCATION, the code location and the spec location, as the [ProjectLocationsScope](../../project-locations/index.md#project-locations-scope) says
- HARNESS_DIRECTORY, the directory of the harness in use
- SPEC_READING, the spec-reading prompt, injected where it is written
- PITON_FLUENCY_FILE, the path of the fluency file, from the project directory, as the pitonFluency below says
- UNDERSTANDING_FILE, the path of the task's understanding file

SPEC_READING is filled in first, so the placeholders it holds are filled in too; then the others, before the prompt is compiled, but UNDERSTANDING_FILE, which is filled in as the prompt is sent, once the task's history record is named, so a prompt sent from the queue is given its own. A question from the Ask tab has no understanding file, and UNDERSTANDING_FILE is filled in with nothing. Each can be moved or removed, like any other text of a template.
Every path a placeholder is filled in with points where the run that is sent it finds that file, whether it runs on the host or in a container, as the [ContainerEnvironmentScope](../../container-environment/index.md#container-environment-scope) says. So each is written relative to the project directory, the directory every run works in, the project directory itself on the host and `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl` in a container: CODE_LOCATION and SPEC_LOCATION as `./` and the location's path, as `./spec`, HARNESS_DIRECTORY as the harness's directory, as `.claude`, and PITON_FLUENCY_FILE and UNDERSTANDING_FILE as their paths, as `.suspense/fluency.md`. None is ever filled in with an absolute path: not the project's path on the host, which a run in a container can't reach, and not `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl`, which a run on the host has no such directory for.
A run fills CODE_LOCATION and SPEC_LOCATION in only with what it can see, as the [ContainerEnvironmentScope](../../container-environment/index.md#container-environment-scope) says. A run of the spec lane, a Spec task or a Chain prompt's spec step, can't see the code location, and fills CODE_LOCATION in with nothing, its instructions and system template alike. A question can see the code location and the spec location, both read only, and fills both in. A run of the code lane, a Code task, a Chain prompt's code step, or a Freeform task, runs on the host and fills both in, as ever.
A paragraph that held nothing but a placeholder filled in with nothing goes with it. A paragraph holding CODE_LOCATION or SPEC_LOCATION filled in with nothing goes too, whatever else it says, so no prompt names, or tells the harness to keep off, a location its run can't see. A paragraph holding PITON_FLUENCY_FILE, filled in with nothing, goes too, whatever else it says, so a sentence pointing at a fluency file there is none of is never sent. A template left with nothing but blank space once filled in gives nothing at all.
HARNESS_DIRECTORY is the directory the harness that runs the prompt, as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says, reads its agentic Markdown and reference files from, written without a leading ./: .claude for Claude Code, .opencode for OpenCode, and .codex for Codex, the directories the [NewProjectScope](../../new-project/index.md#new-project-scope) names for them.

#### Reading The Spec

In every mode, the harness learns what the spec says from its compiled reference, the Markdown the spec build writes under HARNESS_DIRECTORY's reference folder, where inheritance, expressions, and links are already resolved, or, for one thing, from what `piton slice` prints for it with the adapter of the harness in use. It never reads the Piton source under the spec location to learn what the spec says. To a run that can see the spec location, the system template and the spec-reading prompt say so, and name the spec location only as where edits to the spec go. A question sees the spec location too, read only, so it can run `piton slice` there, and is told the same: that the spec is read from the compiled reference or from what `piton slice` prints, never from the Piton source. A question makes no edits, so the Ask instructions name the spec location for what it is, the spec's Piton source, that `piton slice` reads, which a question never changes, and nothing told to a question says or suggests that it may edit the spec. A run that can't see the spec location is told only that the spec is read from the compiled reference, with nothing about the spec source.

#### Writing The Spec

Only Spec, and a Chain prompt's first step, which writes the spec, work on the Piton source. Their instructions say to open a .pi file only to change it, since a harness may need a file read before it can edit it, and, once the edits are made, to run `piton build` and check the result in the refreshed reference rather than by reading the source again.

#### Piton Fluency

The Piton fluency, what `piton agent --print-fluency` prints, run in the project directory, is how Piton is written. It is never part of the system prompt: only work that writes Piton is pointed at it.
It is written to the fluency file, `.suspense/fluency.md` in the project's data, as the [ProjectDataScope](../../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says, each time the application runs a spec build in the project, as the [SpecBuildScope](../../spec-build/index.md#spec-build-scope) says, so it keeps in step with the project's piton and its FLUENCY_PROMPT.md. A Spec or Chain prompt sent before the file has ever been written has it written before the prompt is compiled. What it prints is written as text, never read as Piton, but for the project directory's absolute path on the host wherever it appears in it, which is written as `.` instead, a path within it as relative to it, as `./spec`, so the file holds no path a run in a container can't reach.
PITON_FLUENCY_FILE stands for the file's path. The Spec instructions and the Chain instructions, for a Chain prompt's first step, say, on a paragraph of their own, to read that file once in the conversation before creating or editing any .pi file. A Code task sent to Spec is pointed at it through the Spec instructions, as any Spec prompt is. The Code and Ask instructions, and the spec-to-code prompt given to a Chain prompt's code step, never mention it.
Where `piton` isn't installed, or printing the fluency fails, no file is written, and PITON_FLUENCY_FILE is filled in with nothing, so the paragraph pointing at it is left out.

#### Spec Reading

The spec-reading prompt explains how to read the spec before executing anything, as the readingTheSpec above says: from the compiled reference, reference links in the prompt being the spec for what they name, each read before anything it covers is changed. It is injected into the system template wherever SPEC_READING is written, and may itself use every placeholder but SPEC_READING, which in it is left as written. One left with nothing but blank space leaves SPEC_READING filled in with nothing. Like the templates, each project has its own, saved with its data, as the [ProjectDataScope](../../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says, in spec-reading.md beside them, and edited in the [SettingsWindowScope](../../settings-window/index.md#settings-window-scope); with no file yet the project uses its default.

#### Code To Spec

The code-to-spec prompt is given to a Code task sent to Spec, as the [PromptSendingScope](../sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says, after the Spec instructions. It may use every placeholder the instructions may, filled in the same way, and two of its own: CODE_PROMPT, filled in with the code task's prompt as it was typed, and CODE_RESULT, with the code task's final output, or with a line saying the code task left none. What fills them in is taken as text, never read as Piton. Like the spec-reading prompt, each project has its own, saved with its data in code-to-spec.md beside the templates, and edited in the [SettingsWindowScope](../../settings-window/index.md#settings-window-scope); with no file yet the project uses its default.
The spec-to-code prompt is given in the same way to the code step a Chain prompt hands on to, after the Code instructions, with SPEC_PROMPT and SPEC_RESULT, the Chain prompt as it was typed and its spec step's final output, saved in spec-to-code.md.

#### Saving

Each project has its own system template, instructions, and injected prompts, saved with its data, as the [ProjectDataScope](../../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says, a Markdown file each, system.md for the system template, code.md, combined.md for Chain, spec.md, and ask.md for the modes, and edited in the [SettingsWindowScope](../../settings-window/index.md#settings-window-scope). One with no file yet gives its default.

#### Understanding File

Each Code, Chain, or Spec task has an understanding file: the short list of constraints the harness has taken from the spec for it, which the [RightSidebarScope](../../../ui/components/right-sidebar/index.md#right-sidebar-scope) shows as it changes. It is saved beside the task's history record, with the same name and the extension `.understanding.md`, written by the harness itself. Nothing else writes it, and nothing is there until the harness writes it. Each constraint links to the compiled reference file it comes from, never to the spec's source.

#### Defaults

The defaults are the prompts saved in this application's own repository, in its `.suspense/system-prompts` directory, named as a project's are. They are the source of truth for the defaults, and are baked into the application when it is built, so a build always ships with whatever those files say, and changing them changes the defaults the next build has. A build can't be made without them.
The system template's default says what the project is, where its code is and where its spec is, each on a paragraph of its own, so the one a run can't see goes, that each prompt starts with a <task-instructions> block saying what that prompt is for and what it may change, and then SPEC_READING on a paragraph of its own. It holds no fluency.
The spec-reading prompt's default says:
Read the spec from its compiled reference under ${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference, where inheritance, expressions, and links are already resolved, or, for one thing, from what `piton slice` prints for it with this harness's adapter.

Never read the .pi source under ${SPEC_LOCATION} to learn what the spec says; that is only where edits to the spec go.

Before executing anything, read the spec it touches. Links to ${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference/... in the prompt are the spec for what they name. Read each one you need before changing anything it covers. Don't re-read something you've already read.
The Spec and Chain defaults have, after what the mode is for, on a paragraph of its own:
Before creating or editing any .pi file, read ${PITON_FLUENCY_FILE} once in this conversation, unless you already have: it is how Piton is written.
and then, on another:
Open a .pi file only to change it. Once you have changed the spec, run `piton check` and fix every error it reports, then run `piton build` and check the result in the refreshed reference under ${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference, not by reading the source again. Never finish with a spec that `piton check` or `piton build` reports errors in.
The Code, Chain, and Spec defaults then end with, on a paragraph of its own:
Before changing anything, write the constraints this task must meet to ${UNDERSTANDING_FILE}, and keep it current as you read more of the spec. It is a Markdown list and nothing else: one line per constraint, at most twelve, each a single short, specific statement of what must be true, written as a link to the compiled reference file it comes from, such as `- [The chain tab has no bottom border in combined mode](${HARNESS_DIRECTORY}/reference/scope/prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chain)`. Only list what the spec says; leave out anything you are deciding yourself. Replace a constraint when you learn it was wrong rather than adding another.
The Ask default says what a question is for, and that it changes nothing, and, on a paragraph of its own, that SPEC_LOCATION is the spec's Piton source, there for `piton slice`, which the question reads the spec through, read only and never edited, and never read directly to learn what the spec says. Since a question can see the spec location, that paragraph is always sent with it.
The Ask default then says, on a paragraph of its own, how an answer hands back prompts and questions in the forms the [AskConversationScope](../ask-conversation/index.md#ask-conversation-scope) shows as cards:
When your answer suggests a prompt for the user to send, write it as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-prompt` and the mode it is for, one of `code`, `chain`, `spec`, `ask`, or `freeform`, such as ```` ```suspense-prompt chain ````, holding only the prompt's text, ready to send. When you need the user to answer something before you can go on, write the question as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-question`, the question on its first lines and then, if there are answers to pick from, one per line, each starting with `- `. Use these blocks only for prompts and questions meant for the user, never for code or examples.
The Spec and Chain defaults never name the code location, and the Code default names the spec location only on a paragraph of its own, which goes where the run can't see it.
The defaults are only where a project starts, and what resetting a prompt puts back. A project whose prompts were saved before a default changed keeps them as they are.

# Baked System Prompts Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

The prompts the application gives the harness for its own work, rather than a prompt someone writes, written in Piton and built into the application.

### Shape

#### Description

The prompts are Piton files in the repository's system-prompts folder, one for each piece of the application's own work.

#### Prompts

- divergence.pi, for the two agents of a divergence analysis
- generate-skills.pi, for ranking the spec's scopes for skills
- rescope.pi, for finding concepts to extract into scopes, and for the refactoring prompt sent for those chosen
- run-targets.pi, for finding how the project is built, run, and tested
- commit-note.pi, for a finished task's commit note
- commit-message.pi, for writing a commit message
- file-search.pi, for the palette's search for a file by description
- prompt-title.pi, for titling a task or question so its hidden anchor can be named after it

#### Writing

Each is an exported anchor, its text written as prose, one property for each paragraph or piece the application puts together, such as a heading above a list of files. What the application fills in is a name in angle brackets, such as <codeRoot>, so it isn't taken as Piton.

#### Building

They are compiled with `piton compile` when the application is built, and built into it: changing one changes what the next build sends, and a prompt that doesn't compile fails the build, with piton's error. Each build keeps what it compiled in system-prompts/compiled.json, with the source, so the application still builds where `piton` isn't installed, such as on CI, from the prompts as last compiled, saying so.

#### Mode Prompts

The system prompts each chat mode sends are not among them: see the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts-scope).

The defaults are the prompts saved in this application's own repository, in its `.suspense/system-prompts` directory, named as a project's are. # Baked System Prompts Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

The prompts the application gives the harness for its own work, rather than a prompt someone writes, written in Piton and built into the application.

### Shape

#### Description

The prompts are Piton files in the repository's system-prompts folder, one for each piece of the application's own work.

#### Prompts

- divergence.pi, for the two agents of a divergence analysis
- generate-skills.pi, for ranking the spec's scopes for skills
- rescope.pi, for finding concepts to extract into scopes, and for the refactoring prompt sent for those chosen
- run-targets.pi, for finding how the project is built, run, and tested
- commit-note.pi, for a finished task's commit note
- commit-message.pi, for writing a commit message
- file-search.pi, for the palette's search for a file by description
- prompt-title.pi, for titling a task or question so its hidden anchor can be named after it

#### Writing

Each is an exported anchor, its text written as prose, one property for each paragraph or piece the application puts together, such as a heading above a list of files. What the application fills in is a name in angle brackets, such as <codeRoot>, so it isn't taken as Piton.

#### Building

They are compiled with `piton compile` when the application is built, and built into it: changing one changes what the next build sends, and a prompt that doesn't compile fails the build, with piton's error. Each build keeps what it compiled in system-prompts/compiled.json, with the source, so the application still builds where `piton` isn't installed, such as on CI, from the prompts as last compiled, saying so.

#### Mode Prompts

The system prompts each chat mode sends are not among them: see the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts-scope).

##### Spec

A Spec task, or a Chain prompt's spec step or spec follow-up: the spec location, read and write; the compiled reference, the harness directory's reference folder, read and write, so it can run `piton build` itself; the project's `.piton` directory, which holds the build's manifest of the files it owns, read and write, for the same reason, bound in from the project itself, never an empty, temporary, or copied one, so the manifest a build in the container starts from is the host's, and what it writes there is the host's next build's, the application creating the directory in the project first where it isn't there; the fluency file, read only; piton.config.pi, read only; and the task's understanding file, read and write. Never the code location: in its place, an empty scratch directory, writable, that nothing else sees and that goes with the container, so `piton build` finds the code location it places the shape's guidance in.

##### Question

A question from the Ask tab: the code location, the spec location, the compiled reference, and piton.config.pi, each read only, so it can run `piton slice` in its container. Nothing is writable but the harness's own volume and the questions' sessions folder. Where one of the code location and the spec location holds the other, both are still mounted, read only, and neither is hidden from the question by the other.

Each run is also given its own conversation's sessions folder, read and write, as Volumes says, and nothing of any other conversation's.
Nothing else is ever mounted: not the user's home directory, the user's own skills, MCP servers, or user-level CLAUDE.md, and not the project's git directory. A location that holds another, as a code location holding the spec or the project data, is mounted without the one it holds, so the one held is never seen through it, unless the run is given the one held as well, as a question is given both the code location and the spec location.
A task's understanding file is mounted on its own, never the history folder it is in, so a run sees no other task's record. Since a file has to be there to be mounted, the application writes it empty just before the run, and an empty understanding file is shown as one not written yet is.

There are five modes, and wherever they are listed, they are in this order.

#### Modes

- Code: changes the code, leaving the spec as it is; a subtle red

#### Colours

Whatever shows a mode, or something sent in it, takes the mode's colour, a tint of the [ThemeScope](../../../ui/theme/index.md#theme-scope)'s hue of that name, readable in both light and dark mode. Chain is Code and Spec together, so wherever it shows Code and Spec as well, both are purple: the colour midway between Code's and Spec's. #### Tasks

A prompt sent in Code, Chain, Spec, or Freeform is a task, sent as the [PromptSendingScope](../sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) says. #### Questions

A prompt sent in Ask is a question. It runs straight away, alongside any task and any other question, and never queues, builds the spec, or adds a commit note. Questions carry on a conversation of their own, apart from the tasks', as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../harness-integration/index.md#harness-integration-scope) says.

A prompt sent in Freeform is passed to the harness exactly as it was typed, with anything attached to it, and nothing else: no system prompt, no hidden anchor compiled from it, no spec built ahead of it, no slices, whatever the Slice toggle says, and no understanding file. content.text:
I added a "Suspense fluency" to the spec: a file explaining how Suspense works, which Code, Chain, Spec and Ask prompts are pointed at but Freeform never is. `piton check` reports no problems, `piton build` wrote 79 files, and the new sections appear in the refreshed reference.

**Existing projects won't get it on their own.** The spec already says a project keeps its saved mode prompts when a default changes. So the project you have in mind will only point its Ask at the fluency once you reset its Ask prompt in Settings, or add the paragraph by hand. New projects get it automatically. If you'd rather it reach existing projects without a reset, the spec could insert the pointer for every non-Freeform mode instead of relying on the saved prompt. Say if you want that.

## What changed in the spec

**1. New `#suspense-fluency` section** in `.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md`
- **What it is:** a short, harness-facing description of Suspense, the same for every project.
- **Where it comes from:** the source is `suspense-fluency.md` in this repo's `.suspense/system-prompts/`, built into the app like the default prompts. A build can't be made without it, and projects can't edit it.
- **Where it's written:** to `.suspense/suspense-fluency.md` in each project, before any Code, Chain, Spec or Ask prompt is compiled, whenever the file is missing or out of date. It holds plain text with no placeholders or machine paths.
- **What it covers:**
  - the five modes and what each may change;
  - the two lanes and the queue, and that questions run straight away;
  - a Chain prompt's spec step, then its code step;
  - that Suspense adds the `<task-instructions>` block itself, so a prompt written for a mode is only the user's request;
  - how to write a good prompt for each mode;
  - the `suspense-prompt` and `suspense-question` blocks;
  - the understanding file;
  - that the user can cancel, resend, send to the other mode, and start a new conversation.
- **What it leaves out:** anything specific to one project, and anything a mode's own instructions already say.

**2. A new placeholder and default paragraph** in the same file
- **`SUSPENSE_FLUENCY_FILE`** is added to the placeholders (`#templates`). It is filled in with a relative path, and its paragraph is dropped when the file can't be written.
- **Defaults (`#defaults`):** the Code, Chain, Spec and Ask defaults gain a paragraph of their own. It tells the run to read that file once per conversation when the work is about Suspense, or when it is to write a prompt or question for the user. Freeform never mentions it, and the Piton fluency rules are unchanged.

**3. Supporting changes**
- **Containers** (`.claude/reference/scope/container-environment/index.md`, `#spec` and `#question`): Spec runs and questions mount the Suspense fluency file read only.
- **Project data** (`.claude/reference/scope/project-data/index.md`, `#contents` and `#machine-only`): `suspense-fluency.md` is listed, and counts as belonging to one machine.
- **Modes** (`.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/modes/index.md#system-prompts`): every mode but Freeform is pointed at the Suspense fluency.
- **Settings window** (`.claude/reference/scope/settings-window/index.md`): the placeholder help now explains `SUSPENSE_FLUENCY_FILE`.

The constraints are in `.suspense/history/1791125882-RequireSuspenseFluencyForPromptModes.understanding.md`.

## Anchors the code should follow
- `ModeSystemPromptsScope`: `#suspense-fluency`, `#templates`, `#defaults`. Also write the new default file and update `code.md`, `combined.md`, `spec.md` and `ask.md` in `.suspense/system-prompts`.
- `ContainerEnvironmentScope`: `#spec`, `#question`
- `ProjectDataScope`: `#contents`, `#machine-only`
- `PromptModesScope`: `#system-prompts`
- `SettingsWindowScope`: the placeholder description

The Gmail, Google Calendar and Google Drive connectors still need authorizing in your claude.ai connector settings before they can be used. None of them were needed here.
